message.content:
The **first artificial satellite** was **Sputnik 1**, launched by the Soviet Union on **October 4, 1957**; it was about the size of a beach ball and weighed about **184 pounds (83.6 kg)**[1][5]. By contrast, the **latest satellites** are vastly more advanced, but the phrase “latest” is too broad to identify one single satellite without specifying a date, agency, or mission type[2][5].

A simple comparison:

| Feature | Sputnik 1 | Typical latest satellite |
|---|---|---|
| **Launch era** | 1957[1][5] | Modern era, with ongoing launches every year |
| **Size** | Beach-ball-sized, about 22.8 inches in diameter[5] | Can range from small CubeSats to large multi-ton spacecraft |
| **Mass** | 83.6 kg / 183.9 lb[5] | Often far more capable, with much larger or more specialized payloads |
| **Function** | Basic radio transmitter; no scientific instrument suite[2][5] | Imaging, communications, navigation, weather, Earth observation, scientific research, and more |
| **Impact** | Opened the Space Age[2][5] | Builds on decades of progress in satellite technology |

If you want, I can also compare **Sputnik 1** with the **most recent satellite launched by NASA, SpaceX, Russia, China, or ESA**.
